opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is that you have to genuinely solve a real problem. A lot of people think open source is about putting code on GitHub, but code alone doesn't build a community. When we started projects like XGBoost and later TVM, the starting point was always that we ourselves had a pain point, and we believed other people had the same pain point. If the thing you build is actually useful, people will come and try it. That's the seed.

But usefulness only gets people in the door. What makes them stay and believe in it is something different. I think a big part of it is openness in the real sense, not just an open license, but open decision making. People need to feel that if they contribute, their voice actually matters, that this isn't one company's or one lab's project where outsiders are just free labor. With TVM, for example, we eventually moved it to the Apache Software Foundation, and part of the reason was to make it very clear that the project belongs to the community. We put a lot of effort into things like public RFCs, discussing design on the forums instead of in private meetings, and promoting committers based on merit, regardless of where they work.

The second thing is being welcoming to newcomers. Early on, every single contributor matters a lot. When someone sends their first pull request, how you respond really determines whether they come back. If you're dismissive, or you let it sit for weeks, you lose them. If you take the time to review it carefully, explain things, and say thank you, there's a good chance that person becomes a long-term contributor, and maybe later a maintainer who helps the next newcomer. That's how a community grows: people helping people, not just one core team doing everything.

And the third thing, which I think is underrated, is having a shared vision. People want to be part of something bigger than fixing a bug. For machine learning systems, the vision we kept talking about was making ML available to everyone, on every kind of hardware, not just a few big players with huge clusters. When people believe in that direction, they're willing to put in their evenings and weekends, and they see their contribution as part of a larger story.

So, to sum it up: solve a real problem, make it truly open in governance, treat every contributor with respect, and give people a vision worth believing in. None of these is a trick. It takes a lot of patience and consistency over many years. But when it works, the community becomes much stronger than any individual or any single organization could be.

r001.rationale: The response discusses openness, welcoming contributors, and sustained effort, but does not state that abandoning project maintenance can undermine trust in the creators’ later projects.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that you can't really engineer belief directly. What you can do is build something that solves a real problem for real people, and then be relentlessly open about how it's built and where it's going.

When we started XGBoost, I wasn't trying to build a community. I was trying to make gradient boosting fast enough to actually use on the problems I cared about. The community came because people on Kaggle found it worked, won competitions with it, and then wanted to contribute back. That order matters. Usefulness comes first, and the community forms around usefulness. If you start by trying to build a community around something that doesn't yet deliver value, people can tell.

The second thing is that you have to lower the barrier to contribution as much as possible, and you have to genuinely give ownership away. In the early days of MXNet and later Apache TVM, a lot of what I spent time on wasn't writing code. It was writing design documents, responding to issues quickly, and making sure that when someone sent a pull request, they got thoughtful feedback within a day or two instead of silence. Silence kills communities faster than anything else. If a student in another country spends a weekend fixing a bug and nobody responds, they won't come back.

Related to that, you need to be willing to let the project become something different from what you originally imagined. With TVM, the direction shifted significantly based on what hardware vendors and researchers actually needed. If I had insisted on my original vision, it would have stayed a research prototype. Part of building belief is showing people that their input actually changes the project. Governance structure helps here too, which is why we brought TVM into the Apache Software Foundation. It signals that the project doesn't belong to one person or one company.

The third thing, and this one is harder to talk about, is technical taste and consistency. People believe in a project when its design feels coherent, when abstractions compose cleanly, and when the maintainers say no to things that would compromise that. A community needs to trust that the core will remain solid. That means sometimes rejecting contributions, which feels bad, but doing it with clear reasoning and respect builds more trust than accepting everything.

And finally, I'd say patience and teaching. A lot of open-source maintainers burn out because they treat every issue as a demand. I've found it helps to think of the project partly as education. Every design document, every tutorial, every well-explained code review is teaching someone how to think about the problem. Those people become your next maintainers. That's really how you get a community that outlasts you, which should be the goal.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how silence and poor project stewardship can damage trust in a community, but it does not say that abandoning maintenance undermines trust in the creators’ subsequent projects.

astra-6.text:
I think it starts with solving a problem that people actually care about. That gives them a reason to use the project. But for people to contribute, they also need to feel that they can help shape it.

So it’s important to listen, to explain why decisions are made, and to give contributors ownership. When someone brings an idea, can you work with them to develop it? Can they eventually become someone who leads that part of the project?

That takes consistency. You build trust through many small interactions—answering questions, reviewing contributions, following through on what you say. Over time, you want people to feel, “This isn’t just somebody else’s project that I’m helping with. This is our project.” I think that sense of shared ownership is what makes a community last.

r001.rationale: The response says consistent follow-through builds trust, but does not state that abandoning maintenance can undermine trust in the creators’ subsequent projects.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to build something that people find useful. People usually come to an open-source project because they have a problem to solve. But whether they stay depends on whether they feel they can participate and make a difference.

So you need to listen, welcome contributions, and give people ownership. If somebody brings an idea, can they help shape the direction of the project? Can they grow from a user into a contributor, and eventually into someone who leads part of the community?

Trust also takes consistency. It comes from how you make decisions, how you handle disagreements, and whether you follow through. Over time, you want people to feel, “This is our project. I can help build its future.”

r001.rationale: The response discusses usefulness, participation, ownership, and consistent decision-making, but never says that abandoning maintenance undermines trust in the creators’ later projects.
